maker: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes
title: Friar Pedro Shoots El Maragato as His Horse Runs Off
description: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
shortDescription: Francisco de Goya explored satirical and popular aspects of Spanish life. This work, from a series about the notorious criminal El Maragato, features his capture. After escaping prison, El Maragato spent two months stealing food, guns, and money before trying to take Friar Pedro de Saldivia and other people hostage. The friar outsmarted the bandit, however, seizing his gun and shooting him in the thigh.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: The Annunciation
description: Jean Hey (Master of Moulins; Netherlandish, c. 1480-c.1504)
shortDescription: Jean Hey, known as the Master of Moulins, was a leading painter in 15th-century France. Here, he captured the moment the archangel Gabriel announced to Mary that she would give birth to a son. The painting once formed the right side of an altarpiece, with the left side depicting Mary’s own Immaculate Conception and a central section, now lost, featuring the enthroned Virgin and Child.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: The Assumption of the Virgin
description: El Greco (Doménikos Theotokópoulos; Greek, active in Spain, 1541–1614)
shortDescription: This painting was the central element of an altarpiece that was El Greco’s ﬁrst major Spanish commission and large public work. The Virgin ﬂoats upward on the crescent moon, a symbol of her purity, while the apostles express amazement and concern. El Greco’s broad brushstrokes and bold color made this painting a favorite of modern artists such as Pablo Picasso and Mary Cassatt.
creditLine: Gift of Nancy Atwood Sprague in memory of Albert Arnold Sprague

title: Cupid Chastised
shortDescription: This dramatic scene by Bartolomeo Manfredi shows Mars, the god of war, beating Cupid for having caused his affair with Venus, the goddess of love. The sheer physicality of the figures as well as the bold illumination from the left further the work's dynamism. The composition is on one level a tale of domestic disturbance but also symbolizes the eternal conflict between love and war.
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection

title: Cabin in the Cotton
shortDescription: A celebrated African American artist of the mid-20th century, self-taught painter Horace Pippin began painting as therapy, hoping to regain mobility in his right arm, which was injured during WWI. While this work hung in a Philadelphia shoe repair shop, it caught the attention of artists, critics, and gallerists. It is considered an exemplar of the artist's vivid, saturated palette and feeling for intense pattern.
medium: Oil on cotton, mounted on Masonite
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Thomas F. Pick and Mary P. Hines in memory of their mother Frances W. Pick

title: The Advance-Guard, or The Military Sacrifice (The Ambush)
shortDescription: Frederic Remington, famous for his dynamic compositions of frontier life, presented mythic, romanticized views of the American West. Here, a cavalry scout, shot by an unseen Souix warrior, slumps over his horse while the troops behind him flee the ambush. Like most of his work, it was created for a white audience who understood the West as a place of both danger and opportunity.

title: The Garden of Palazzo Contarini dal Zaffo
shortDescription: This painting by Francesco Guardi, an 18th-century landscape painter renowned for his inventive city views, depicts a luxurious Venetian green space. Elegant couples stroll, while a ballgame takes place in the distance and a single gondola slides across the lagoon. Guardi's city scenes were particularly popular with wealthy travelers making the grand tour of Europe as evidence of their extravagant trips.
creditLine: Gift of Marion and Max Ascoli Fund

title: Stoke-by-Nayland
shortDescription: John Constable produced this full-size oil sketch for an unrealized painting near the end of his life. Its subject—the countryside of Constable's youth in Suffolk, England—was one of the artist's favorites. To achieve the effect of sparkling wetness and fresh earth and air, Constable painted with a palette knife, flecking the surface with white highlights as he sketched and scraped the picture into existence.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection

title: I'timad-ud-Daula's Tomb at Agra
medium: Watercolor on paper watermarked J. Whatman with pencil, pen, ink and gold
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Friends of Indian and Islamic Art of The Art Institute of Chicago

title: Pastoral Scene
shortDescription: This painting of a half-naked boy holding a basket of grapes has been interpreted as the infant Bacchus, the god of wine, although Piazzetta, one of Vencie's leading painters, made no reference in his description. The artist was probably responding to his patron’s taste for pastoral scenes, a genre that appealed to middle- and upper-class city dwellers for its idealized views of rural life.
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection

title: Equestrienne (At the Cirque Fernando)
shortDescription: This work, set at a circus, captures the tense moment in which a female trick rider prepares to stand up on her horse and leap through a paper hoop held by a clown. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec may have based the rider, dressed in a tutu of gauze and sequins, on Suzanne Valadon, a former circus performer, model, and artist with whom he had a relationship.

title: Old Man with a Gold Chain
shortDescription: In his character studies, Rembrandt explored the effect of a single figure, made dramatic through the use of rich, subtle lighting and costumes, which the artist collected to transform his models. Here, the gold chain and steel gorget suggest an honored military career, while the plumed beret evokes an earlier time. The unidentified sitter, once thought to be the artist’s father, was a favorite model.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection

title: Water Lilies
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: The Herring Net
shortDescription: One of the most influential American painters of the 19th century, Winslow Homer is known for his dynamic depictions of both upper-class leisure pursuits and nature's power and beauty. The paintings he created after 1882 focus almost exclusively on humankind’s contest with nature. Here, Homer depicted the heroic efforts of fishermen hauling in an abundant catch of herring while steadying their boat amid turbulent swells.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare
shortDescription: The Impressionists frequently paid tribute to the modern aspects of Paris, depicting scenes of grand boulevards and modern constructions. Monet made 12 paintings of the Gare Saint-Lazare. Here, he focused on the glass-and-iron train shed, where he found an appealing combination of artificial and natural effects: the rising steam of locomotives trapped within the structure and daylight penetrating the large, glazed sections of the roof.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: Richard Bill
shortDescription: The Scottish-born painter John Smibert studied in London and Italy before settling in Boston in 1728. His skills as a trained formal portraitist were in great demand among Boston's wealthy and powerful colonists. Here, he depicted Richard Bill, a prosperous merchant and politically involved citizen. The large ship, visible through the window in the background, combined with Bill's elegant clothing, suggests his success and prestige.

title: The Bay of Marseille, Seen from L'Estaque
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: Bar-room Scene
shortDescription: William Sidney Mount was one of the first American artists to specialize in scenes of everyday life. Here, Mount portrayed a boisterous group of patrons in a country tavern. Standing in the back corner is an African American figure who, as a free black man in 1830s New York, may have been able to frequent the tavern but did not participate fully in this community.
creditLine: The William Owen Goodman and Erna Sawyer Goodman Collection

creditLine: Gift of Arthur M. Wood, Sr. in memory of Pauline Palmer Wood

title: At the Moulin Rouge
shortDescription: Toulouse-Lautrec made a career depicting colorful personalities from Parisian cabarets and dance halls like the Moulin Rouge. He populated this painting with that nightclub's regulars, including himself—the diminutive figure in the center background. Dancer La Goulue arranges her hair behind the table where Jane Avril, another performer, socializes. Singer May Milton peers out from the painting's right edge, her face harshly lit and acid green.

title: Portrait of Jean Gros (recto); Coat of Arms of Jean Gros (verso)
description:
Rogier van der Weyden (Netherlandish, c. 1399–1464)
Workshop of Rogier van der Weyden (Netherlandish, c. 1399–1464)
shortDescription: This portrait was once part of a diptych. The sitter—identifiable through his coat of arms, personal motto, and initials on the panel's back—is Jean Gros, an administrator to the future duke of Burgundy. His prayerful gaze was originally directed at the other panel depicting Mary and the infant Jesus. Rogier van der Weyden created similar diptychs for the Burgundian court's highest level of patrons.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: Self-Portrait
shortDescription: Van Gogh’s face is as well known as his art—in fact, it is inseparable from it. The artist painted more than 35 self-portraits over his lifetime. This one was created in Paris under the influence of Seurat and pointillism. The intense dabs of paint and color, anchored by his eyes, create a turbulent energy, giving the viewer a deep sense of the artist’s presence.
medium: Oil on artist's board, mounted on cradled panel

title: The Girl by the Window
shortDescription: Edvard Munch’s life and art have come to epitomize modern notions of anxiety. Created the same year as his renowned The Scream , this painting depicts a young girl in her nightgown gazing out at the city from her darkened room. The steep angle of the floor and the deep shadows that obliterate almost everything in the room create an unsettling and enigmatic scene.
creditLine: Searle Family Trust and Goldabelle McComb Finn endowments; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection

title: The Millinery Shop
shortDescription: When this work was painted, millinery work (hat making) was considered a prestigious trade, elevating the women who succeeded in the business. Degas addressed this subtle shift in the class hierarchy: He gave his milliner a dress nice enough to be worn by an affluent woman, and though she does not wear the expected hat of a high-class lady, Degas playfully positioned the hat with green trimmings so it seems to sit atop the woman’s head.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection

title: Salome with the Head of Saint John the Baptist
shortDescription: Guido Reni was the most famous and successful Italian painter of his day. This painting depicts Salome receiving the head of John the Baptist on a platter, the gruesome reward she chose for having pleased her stepfather, Herod, by performing a seductive dance. This episode from the New Testament had long been popular in Italian art thanks to its combination of religiosity, violence, and eroticism.
creditLine: Louise B. and Frank H. Woods Purchase Fund

title: Mère Grégoire
shortDescription: Gustave Courbet played a crucial role in the development of modern French Realism. Critics and the public, however, did not easily accept his large, naturalistic, and unsentimental depictions of commonplace, often rural subjects. They called him the “apostle of ugliness.” This painting's subject, Mère Grégoire, was inspired by the heroine of a popular song, the proprietor of a brothel, written in the 1820s.

title: Two Cows and a Young Bull beside a Fence in a Meadow
shortDescription: During his short life, the prolific Dutch painter and etcher Paulus Potter elevated images of cows, oxen, and other domestic animals to majestic emblems of nature. His lavish attention to the physical appearances of such beasts—the varied texture and coloring of their hair, their characteristic poses, their bulky contours—borders on human portraiture and likely derived from drawings he made from life.
creditLine: In loving memory of Harold T. Martin from Eloise W. Martin, wife, and Joyce Martin Brown, daughter; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection; Lacy Armour Endowment; through prior gift of Frank H. and Louise B. Woods

title: The Holy Family with Saints Elizabeth and John the Baptist
shortDescription: Here, Rubens presented a distinctly human take on the figures of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph. They lack the halos that often identify them, and the adult characters wear contemporary Flemish attire. Mary’s exposed breast brings to mind Jesus’s need for physical nourishment as the human son of God. Her central placement underscores the growing veneration of Mary in the Catholic community of the Spanish Netherlands.

title: View of Cotopaxi
creditLine: Gift of Jennette Hamlin in memory of Mr. and Mrs. Louis Dana Webster

title: Beata Beatrix
shortDescription: Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, a circle of Victorian artists united in their regard for medieval aesthetics. Inspired by his namesake, Dante, Rossetti drew parallels in this work between the Italian poet's love for Beatrice and his own affection for his deceased wife and muse, Elizabeth Siddal, a talented artist and writer who died at age 32.

description:
Teotihuacan
Tlacuilapaxco apartment compound, Teotihuacán, Mexico
shortDescription: The ancient Mexican city of Teotihuacan was once the largest city in the Americas. Its pyramid facades and palace interiors were frequently decorated with splendid frescoes. This fragment was part of a cycle painted on the interior walls of an aristocratic palace. It shows a rain priest with a speech-scroll adorned with seashells and plants, indicating a prayer for water and agricultural prosperity.

title: Gian Lodovico Madruzzo
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection

title: Jacques and Berthe Lipchitz
shortDescription: Amedeo Modigliani created his finest paintings between 1914 and his premature death in 1920. Focusing on a limited range of subjects, mainly portraits and nudes, he developed a highly distinctive style of sensitively elongated forms. Sculptor Jacques Lipchitz commissioned Modigliani to paint this portrait on the occasion of his marriage to the poet Berthe Kitrosser as a way of helping his troubled friend financially.

title: Nocturne: Blue and Gold—Southampton Water
shortDescription: In the 1870s James McNeill Whistler took a radical step toward abstraction with his "Nocturnes" series. In keeping with his art-for-art’s-sake creed, these works capture the stillness of evening while evoking the artistry of music. The subject of this work—an inlet along the English Channel—is obscured by the approaching night, allowing Whistler to fully explore the tonal harmonies of darkness.

title: The Beach at Sainte-Adresse
shortDescription: In 1867 Monet stayed with his aunt in Sainte-Adresse, a suburb of the port city of Le Havre in Normandy, where the artist grew up. Monet began the painting outdoors but likely revised it in his studio. Technical analysis of the work revealed that it started as a beach scene of yachts and tourists but ultimately became a view of sailboats and local fishermen.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection

title: Husking Bee, Island of Nantucket
shortDescription: This painting by Eastman Johnson takes its nostalgic theme from rural Nantucket. A timeless evocation of agrarian peace and cooperation, it includes a woman discovering a red ear of corn, which, according to folk tradition, would allow her to kiss the person of her choice. This use of local subject matter combined with an international style was typical of American art around the time of the centennial.
creditLine: Gift of Honoré and Potter Palmer

title: Amédée-David, the Comte de Pastoret
shortDescription: This portrait by French painter Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres depicts the young count Amédée-David de Pastoret at 32 years old. One of several paintings he commissioned from Ingres, the portrait highlights the nobleman’s status and swagger. Posing confidently in his finest garments and wearing a medal of the Order of the Legion of Honor, he gazes directly at the viewer with a stern expression.
creditLine: Estate of Dorothy Eckhart Williams; Robert Allerton, Bertha E. Brown, and Major Acquisitions funds

title: Arrangement in Flesh Color and Brown: Portrait of Arthur Jerome Eddy
Magnolias on Light Blue Velvet Cloth
shortDescription: This painting dates from the later part of Martin Johnson Heade’s long, varied, and peripatetic career. After traveling through the United States, to England and continental Europe, and three different times to Brazil, Heade settled in Saint Augustine, Florida, at the age of 64. There he began painting detailed arrangements of native flowers, including the Cherokee rose, orange blossom, and, as in this work, magnolia.
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Gloria and Richard Manney; Harold L. Stuart Endowment Fund

title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884
shortDescription: For his largest and best-known painting, Georges Seurat depicted Parisians enjoying all sorts of leisurely activities—strolling, lounging, sailing, and fishing—in the park called La Grande Jatte on the River Seine. He used an innovative technique called Pointillism that was inspired by optical and color theory, applying tiny dabs of different colored paint that viewers would see as a single, and Seurat believed, more brilliant hue.

title: Judith
description: Jan Sanders van Hemessen (Netherlandish, active c. 1519–1556)
shortDescription: According to the biblical story, the widow Judith saved her people from being slaughtered by the Assyrian army by infiltrating the tent of the enemy general, Holofernes. She then seduced and beheaded him. Jan van Hemessen's life-size interpretation reflects men's ambivalence toward female agency in 16th-century Netherlands. It celebrates Judith's physical and moral strength but also foregrounds the sexuality that enabled her triumph.

title: Portrait of a Man in Costume
shortDescription: The 18th-century artist Jean-Honoré Fragonard is best known for his lighthearted, amorous subjects. This work, painted in lively brushstrokes, represents another important aspect of his genius—his fantasy portraits, in which he referenced earlier artworks to enliven his own characterizations of patrons and artistic friends. In this instance, Fragonard references a painting of an actor by the Italian Baroque artist Domenico Fetti.
creditLine: Gift of Mary and Leigh Block in honor of John Maxon

title: Fish (Still Life)
shortDescription: This painting, like many of Manet’s still lifes, recalls 17th-century Dutch models. The directness of execution, bold brushwork, and immediacy of vision, however, suggest why the public found Manet’s work so unorthodox and confrontational. While this painting depicts “dead nature” ( nature morte is French for still life), there is nothing still about the work: the produce seems fresh and the handling of the paint vigorous.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection

title: Group Pilgrimage to the Jizo Nun
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment; Margaret Gentles Fund; Purchased with funds provided by Roger L. Weston, George and Roberta Mann, Harlow and Susan Higinbotham, Charles C. Haffner III, James M. and Carol D. Trapp

title: Lozenge Composition with Yellow, Black, Blue, Red, and Gray
shortDescription: Piet Mondrian, a founding member of the international movement De Stijl (the Style), said “the straight line tells the truth.” Deceptively simple, his works are the result of continual tinkering to achieve absolute balance and harmony. In this work, Mondrian rotated a square canvas 90 degrees to create a dynamic relationship between the rectilinear composition and the diagonal lines of the painting's edges.

title: View of Delphi with a Procession
shortDescription: Like other foreign artists drawn to the ruins of antiquity, Claude Lorrain was fascinated with the Roman Empire. This painting of the ancient city of Delphi (in what is now Greece) presents a glowing Mediterranean atmosphere. Here, he evokes a serene, bucolic world akin to the poetic vision of the Roman writer Virgil, depicting the ruins restored to what Lorrain imagined was their original glory.

title: A City Park
shortDescription: William Merritt Chase was one of the most influential painters at the turn of the 20th century. In this painting, which probably depicts Brooklyn’s Tompkins Park, half the canvas is filled by the wide, empty walkway. Its strong diagonal borders carry the eye into the scene. This informal piece, capturing the sparkle of a summer day, affirms the fresh perspective Chase brought to painting scenes like this one.
creditLine: Bequest of Dr. John J. Ireland

title: Hercules and the Lernaean Hydra
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Eugene A. Davidson

title: Mrs. Daniel Hubbard (Mary Greene)
shortDescription: John Singleton Copley garnered considerable success as a portrait painter before the Revolutionary War. The sitter here, Mary Greene Hubbard, was a member of Boston’s merchant class. Her pose, gown, and background were precisely copied from a British engraving of a noblewoman, yet Copley distinguished the work as his own by capturing Hubbard’s unique features and the luxurious fabrics she wears.
creditLine: Art Institute of Chicago Purchase Fund

title: Interrupted Reading
shortDescription: Corot rarely exhibited his late figure paintings like this compelling example, focusing instead on his idyllic landscapes. While here he chose a traditional subject—the muse-like image of a woman reading a book—Corot showed his model pausing and looking up. He also used unconventionally bold brushwork while still delighting in detail—the ribbon in the model’s hair, the delicate earrings, and the deep folds in the skirt.
medium: Oil on canvas, mounted on board

title: The Child's Bath
shortDescription: Known for her sensitive yet unsentimental scenes of women and children, Mary Cassatt was the only American invited to exhibit with the original French Impressionist group. In The Child’s Bath , one of her masterworks, she used cropped forms, bold patterns and outlines, and a flattened perspective, all of which she derived from her study of Japanese woodblock prints.

title: Woman Reading
shortDescription: Édouard Manet was a pivotal figure in the development of Impressionism and modern art. Here, an elegantly dressed Parisian woman reads a magazine, a beer close at hand—a scene that would have struck contemporary viewers as fashionable and modern. While the woman appears to be outdoors, one of Manet’s paintings serves as a backdrop and other props suggest the scene was staged in Manet’s studio.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection

title: Pillars of the Country
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on paper

title: Croquet Scene
shortDescription: One of America’s foremost painters, Winslow Homer began his career as an illustrator. In the late 1860s, he turned to oil painting, depicting figures bathed in sunlight. These early paintings feature scenes of upper-class leisure pursuits—in this case, women and men playing the popular sport of croquet, a game that had recently been introduced to the United States from the British Isles.
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection; Goodman Fund

title: Elizabeth Grant Bankson Beatty (Mrs. James Beatty) and Her Daughter Susan
shortDescription: The first known Black painter to gain professional recognition in the United States, Joshua Johnson was celebrated for his portraits of white middle-class families. The son of a white man and an enslaved woman, Johnson was originally enslaved before becoming free when he came of age. Described as “self-taught” in a newspaper advertisement, he attracted local patrons among the city’s artisan and middle-class families.

title: Arlésiennes (Mistral)
shortDescription: One of 17 canvases that Paul Gauguin completed during a brief and tumultuous visit with Vincent van Gogh in Arles, this powerful and enigmatic painting depicts the public garden directly across from Van Gogh’s house. The painting's large, ﬂat areas of color, arbitrary handling of space, and enigmatic silhouettes exemplify the deliberateness with which Gauguin sought visual harmony and symbolism in his work.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection

title: Early Morning, Tarpon Springs
shortDescription: Over his career, Georges Inness became less interested in detailed paintings and more interested in "poetic truth," conveying mood and emotion through rich tone and broad handling. He made this painting in Tarpon Springs, Florida, after recently establishing his house and studio there. Through blurred outlines, subtle tonalities, and the solitary figure, Inness evoked the brightening day and peaceful mood of the moment.

title: The Captive Slave (Ira Aldridge)
shortDescription: This painting by John Philip Simpson is both a powerful abolitionist statement and a striking portrait of the celebrated Shakespearean actor Ira Aldridge. A freeborn American, Aldridge became the first Black man to play Othello on the London stage in 1833. Simpson’s painting highlights Aldridge’s gifts of expression as a tragic actor.
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mary Winton Green, Dan and Sara Green Cohan, Howard and Lisa Green and Jonathan and Brenda Green, in memory of David Green

title: Landscape with the Ruins of the Castle of Egmond
shortDescription: The deteriorating Castle of Egmond was a visible reminder of the Dutch struggle for independence: it was sacrificially destroyed during the revolt against Spain more than 80 years before Jacob van Ruisdael produced this painting. Landscape specialists like Van Ruisdael invoked Dutch patriotism by selecting sites representative of the republic, including ruins, windmills, and city views.

title: The Bedroom
shortDescription: In 1888, Van Gogh moved into his own home in Arles, France. He dubbed it the “Studio of the South,” hoping that fellow artists would join him there to work. This is one of three versions he painted of his beloved Arles bedroom. While its vivid palette and dramatic perspective seem to burst with nervous vitality, Van Gogh intended the painting "to express utter repose."

title: Merahi metua no Tehamana (Tehamana Has Many Parents or The Ancestors of Tehamana)
shortDescription: In this portrait, Gauguin depicts the 13-year-old Tahitian girl Tehamana in a missionary dress holding a Samoan fan. A ripe mango alludes to fertility. In the background, Gauguin combined various non-European emblems—glyphs derived from an Easter Island tablet and a female deity inspired by Polynesian and Hindu sources—to build a generic sense of foreignness, transforming Tehamana into the embodiment of his own imagination.
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Charles Deering McCormick

title: Mountain Brook
description: Albert Bierstadt (American, born Solingen, Prussia, now Germany, 1830–1902)
shortDescription: Albert Bierstadt is best remembered for his paintings of the American West, but during his early career, the ambitious artist also created New England landscapes, particularly of the White Mountains, as seen here. When this painting was first exhibited in 1863, critics declared it Bierstadt’s “best work” and praised the artist’s skillful contrast of “light and shade,” which brings a heightened realism to the image.

title: The Nativity
shortDescription: In 1500 Fra (Friar) Bartolommeo left behind his painting career to join a monastery. Four years later he returned to painting, looking to Da Vinci, Raphael, and Michelangelo to form his new, quietly spiritual style. Here, he depicted the Nativity in a traditional, though especially intimate manner. The Virgin kneels humbly gazing at the Christ Child while Joseph assumes a post of restrained wonderment.

title: Processional Cross with Saint Mary Magdalene and a Blessed Hermit
shortDescription: Representative of the early work of Lorenzo Monaco, a monk and leading Florentine painter, this Crucifixion boasts delicate colors and simplified forms that are exceptionally well preserved. The panel has a hole drilled at the base, allowing it to be mounted on a pole and used as a processional cross, likely in the monastic Camaldolese community where Lorenzo had lived and worked.

title: Woman at Her Toilette
shortDescription: Rendered with feathery brushstrokes in shades of lavender, pink, blue, white, and gray, this Impressionist painting captures a subject often explored by male artists of the day but seldom broached by the period's few women artists. Morisot presents a decidely female perspective, intimate yet not eroticized. She signed her name along the bottom of the mirror, as if to suggest that the image in her painting is as ephemeral as a silvery reﬂection.

title: Armida Encounters the Sleeping Rinaldo
shortDescription: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo’s work epitomizes the brilliant exuberance of the Late Baroque style. Internationally renowned, Tiepolo was often commissioned to transform palaces and monasteries in Venice and elsewhere in Italy, as well as in Germany and Spain. This painting and three others at the Art Institute once graced the cabinet of mirrors, a richly decorated room in the Venetian palace of the powerful Cornaro family.

title: Henri Degas and His Niece Lucie Degas (The Artist's Uncle and Cousin)
shortDescription: Perhaps the most subtle portrait painter in the Impressionist group, Edgar Degas painted this double portrait in the mid-1970s. It shows his orphaned first cousin, Lucie, and their uncle Henri, in whose care the girl had recently been placed—two people who are tentatively accepting the circumstances of their new relationship. Having recently lost his own father, Degas addressed his subjects with awareness and sensitivity.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection

title: The Fountains
shortDescription: In his paintings of ruins, Robert embodied French philosopher Denis Diderot's notion that "Everything vanishes, everything dies, only time endures." This work, one of four canvases commissioned for a wealthy financier’s château (all now in the Art Institute's collection), exploits Robert’s typical vocabulary of fictive niches, arches, coffered vaults, colonnades, majestic stairwells, and Roman statuary to create a fantasy of expansive space.

title: Still Life—Strawberries, Nuts, &c.
shortDescription: During Raphaelle Peale’s time, still lifes were relegated to the bottom of the hierarchy of painting subjects. Peale, however, ignored their low status and is now acknowledged as America’s first professional still-life painter and leading practitioner. In this particularly fine example, the rhythmic balance of fruit, nuts, and Chinese-export porcelain is enlivened by the diagonal branch of grapes becoming raisins and an orange leaf.
creditLine: Gift of Jamee J. and Marshall Field

maker: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes
title: Boy on a Ram
description: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
shortDescription: As painter to the king of Spain, Francisco de Goya also designed tapestries for the royal residences. To work out his designs, he first made small oil sketches and followed them with full-scale painted cartoons that served as guides for the king's weavers. This cartoon was produced for a tapestry in a series decorating the dining room in the Royal Palace of El Pardo, outside Madrid.
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Brooks McCormick

title: The Two Disciples at the Tomb
shortDescription: Perhaps the most renowned American painter of religious works at the turn of the 20th century, Tanner moved to France in 1891 to escape the racism that limited his career. This painting depicts an event from the Gospel of Saint John in which Peter and John arrive at Christ’s empty tomb. Peter looks down somberly, while John is transfixed, bathed in a golden light.

title: Landscape with Saint John on Patmos
At Mouquin's
shortDescription: William Glackens here portrayed members of his circle at a New York restaurant. The proprietor’s wife shares a drink with a wealthy playboy and restaurateur, while the artist’s wife and an art critic are reflected in the mirror. By combining portraiture and everyday scenes, Glackens helped usher in a mode of painting suited to the uncertainties and new social activities of modern urban life.

title: Icebound
shortDescription: During the last decade of his life, John Henry Twachtman frequently painted views of the landscape surrounding his home in Greenwich, Connecticut. Almost square in format, this painting’s harmonious composition exemplifies Twachtman’s opinion that “never is nature more lovely than when it is snowing.” He enjoyed depicting the beauty of the frozen terrain, believing that it was conducive to contemplation and regeneration.

title: Still Life with Dead Game, Fruits, and Vegetables in a Market
shortDescription: This overflowing Flemish market stall is enlivened by dead animals splayed on the table, fighting roosters, and a pickpocket. An early example of Frans Snyders’s combination of ornamental still-life elements with secondary figures, this scene might have adorned the dining room of an aristocratic collector. Snyders was the leading Flemish painter of monumental still lifes. He regularly collaborated with his fellow Antwerp artist Peter Paul Rubens.
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection

title: Acrobats at the Cirque Fernando (Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg)
shortDescription: The two girls in this painting by Pierre-Auguste Renoir are Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg, acrobats who performed in the famed Cirque Fernando in Paris. They are depicted clutching oranges tossed to them from the crowd as gifts. Although they are painted standing in the center of a circus ring, Renoir actually painted them in his studio, where he could take full advantage of natural sunlight.

title: Love of Winter
shortDescription: “There has been none of my favorite snow," George Bellows wrote to a friend in January 1914. "I must always paint the snow at least once a year.” Soon after, a blizzard hit New York City, inspiring this painting. The bright colors and broad brushstrokes convey the pleasure and movement of the skaters and onlookers who are out enjoying a New York City winter.

title: Christ Carrying the Cross
shortDescription: In the 1510s, Sebastiano del Piombo traveled to Rome, where he was drawn into the lively competition between the period's two great luminaries, Michelangelo and Raphael. Michelangelo took Sebastiano under his wing, teaching him his monumental style and providing drawings for commissions. This painting represents a popular composition by Piombo, who became one of the most distinguished painters working during the High Renaissance.

title: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
shortDescription: Despite the title, the young women in this painting were not actually sisters. The older girl in the center gazes absently beyond her younger companion, whose red cheeks suggest that she just dashed into the picture. These casual expressions make this “sisterly” moment feel genuine. Renoir juxtaposed the girls’ figures against a dreamy landscape, the basket of yarn evoking an artist’s palette.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection

title: Improvisation No. 30 (Cannons)
description:
Vasily Kandinsky
Born Moscow (formerly Russian Empire, now Russia), 1866; died Neuilly-sur-Seine, France, 1944
shortDescription: In his 1912 book Concerning the Spiritual in Art , Vasily Kandinsky advocated for an art that could move beyond imitation of the physical world, inspiring, as he put it, “vibrations in the soul.” Between 1910 and 1914 he produced a series of “improvisations," which he described as unconscious, spontaneous expressions. This painting—one of his first improvisations—is a standout work within the museum's modern art collection.

title: Distant View of Niagara Falls
shortDescription: By the 19th century, Niagara Falls was already an iconic American landscape, nearly verging on mythical. Thomas Cole visited the landmark in May 1829 and composed this romanticized, autumnal scene the following year. In amplifying the natural grandeur of the American landscape, the artist wilfully ommitted the factories, scenic overlooks, and hotels that populated the area in the early 19th century.

title: Legends of the Yūzū Nembutsu Sect
shortDescription: Commissioned and executed in the mid-14th century, this lengthy horizontal scroll illustrates the founding of the Yūzū Nembutsu sect of Japanese Buddhism. Yūzū Nembutsu means “chanting [Amida’s] name in communion”—a reference to the belief that one person chanting the Amida Buddha’s name would affect all other beings, whether in attaining individual rebirth or allowing souls in hell to be saved.
medium: Handscroll; ink, colors, and gold on paper

title: The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist
shortDescription: These six paintings illustrate scenes from the life of Saint John the Baptist. We see John enter the wilderness to live as a hermit, foretell Christ’s role as redeemer, be imprisoned, and finally be martyred at the request of Salomé, the step-daughter of King Herod. The artist, Giovanni di Paolo, represented figures multiple times to indicate their movement through highly imaginative and stylized settings.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

title: Retable and Frontal of the Life of Christ and the Virgin
shortDescription: This ensemble comprises a retable, which was set up behind the altar table, and a frontal, which decorated the table's front. The work is a testament to the piety of Pedro López de Ayala, a major figure in the political and cultural life of late medieval Spain. For more than 500 years, it decorated his family's funerary chapel in their fortified palace in northern Spain.

title: Movement
shortDescription: Unlike many American artists, Marsden Hartley was more drawn to German Expressionism than to French modernism. This painting, made in Berlin, possesses an energy that evokes both the vibrancy of modern Berlin and movements of music. Like the painter Vasily Kandinsky, Hartley sought to make his work more like music, which he admired for its potential to be purely spiritual and separate from material reality.

title: Isabella Wolff
shortDescription: This portrait depicts Isabella Wolff, one of Sir Thomas Lawrence’s closest friends. Shown contemplating a printed image of the Delphic Sibyl from Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling, Wolff assumes a pose that cleverly echoes another Sibyl from that same work. Sibyls, priestesses of Classical legend who made enigmatic judgments and prophecies, were often pictured according to Western fantasies of the Near East, hence Wolff’s elaborate turban.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection

title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
shortDescription: Considered Caillebotte’s masterpiece, this view of a busy intersection captures both an everyday moment and all that was new in a rapidly changing Paris. The clothes are the latest fashion. The retractable umbrella was just invented. And a decades-long renovation had transformed the medieval streets of Paris into grand boulevards, like the ones seen here. It's a painting you want to walk into.
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection

title: The Interior of the Palm House on the Pfaueninsel Near Potsdam
shortDescription: The work of Carl Blechen, a pivotal ﬁgure in 19th-century German painting, marks a transition from Romanticism to a more realistic view of nature. Inspired in part by his encounter with the Italian landscape and light during a trip he made around 1828 or 1829, Blechen developed a ﬂuid technique that enabled him to capture ﬂeeting atmospheric effects. He often used his landscapes as settings for mysterious ﬁgures, reﬂecting his early contact with Romantic painting and theater.

title: In the Sea
shortDescription: Böcklin’s art had little in common with Impressionism or the academic art of his time. Instead, his depictions of demigods in naturalistic settings interpret themes from Classical mythology. Böcklin also painted mysterious landscapes that made him an important contributor to the international Symbolist movement and appealed to Surrealist artists, like Giorgio de Chirico, who declared, “Each of [Böcklin’s] works is a shock.”

title: Lady Sarah Bunbury Sacrificing to the Graces
shortDescription: As a portrait painter, Sir Joshua Reynolds liked to give his sitters Classical attributes and poses. Dressed in robes, Lady Sarah Bunbury pours a libation of oil as an offering to the Three Graces, positioned behind her. Her fiancé, Charles Bunbury, commissioned this marriage portrait, making her association with the Graces—symbols of fertility and attendants to the Roman goddess of love, Venus—all the more appropriate.
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection

title: Madame de Pastoret and Her Son
shortDescription: The French Revolution probably accounts for this portrait's unfinished state. While David completed the stippled underpainting, he did not create the smooth surface characteristic of his finished paintings. He did not even place a needle and thread in the subject's hand. Objecting to David’s revolutionary ideals, Madame de Pastoret refused the painting but had her adult son purchase the portrait after the artist's death.
creditLine: Clyde M. Carr Fund and Major Acquisitions Endowment

title: Portrait of Mary Adeline Williams
shortDescription: Thomas Eakins first met Mary Adeline Williams when she was a childhood playmate of his sister. Later, the unmarried Williams lived with Eakins and his wife, Susan. Although Eakins’s portrait presents Addie as straight-laced and severe, this is in marked contrast with the active woman Susan Eakins described in her diary, who rode bicycles, went to art exhibitions, and socialized between sittings for the painting.

title: Virgin and Child with the Young Saint John the Baptist
shortDescription: This intimate devotional panel, an early work by Antonio da Correggio, reveals the young artist's evolving style. The distant landscape demonstrates his awareness of Northern European precedents, and the figural composition references the manner of Raphael, while its soft outlines recall Da Vinci. The gentle sensuousness of the figures and the tenderness they show one another, however, are unique to Correggio.

title: The Battle between the Gods and the Giants
shortDescription: The victory of the Olympic gods over the ancient race of giants was a perfect subject for Wtewael to showcase exaggerated athletic poses and striking contrasts of space and light. Painted on copper, this small work almost appears gem-like. Wtewael's self-conscious display of skills was a hallmark of the international style known as Mannerism, which was fashionable in Holland around 1600.
creditLine: Through prior acquisition of the George F. Harding Fund

title: The Fountain, Villa Torlonia, Frascati, Italy
shortDescription: The year 1907 was a turning point for Sargent; the sought-after portraitist stepped away from his successful portraiture career to pursue plein-air landscape painting. This work, depicting his traveling companions and fellow artists Wilfrid and Jane Emmet de Glehn, captures that moment of transition. Combining landscape and portraiture, the composition speaks to friendship and painterly pursuits while also celebrating color, light, and movement.

title: Saint George and the Dragon
shortDescription: Bernat Martorell was one of the greatest painters in Catalonia, Spain, during the first half of the 15th century. Here, he rendered a frequently depicted episode from the popular legend of Saint George, in which the model Christian knight saves a town and rescues a beautiful princess. George’s halo and armor and the scaly dragon are richly modeled with raised stucco decoration.
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Richard E. Danielson and Mrs. Chauncey McCormick

title: The Combat of the Giaour and Hassan
shortDescription: This colorful scene was inspired by a poem from Lord Byron’s “oriental tales,” a popular series of romances. Both the poem and painting are examples of 19th-century Europeans’ interest in fantastical and often violent depictions of Middle Eastern, North African, and Asian cultures, which reinforced colonialist aims. Delacroix began painting Orientalist subjects early in his career, though he did not visit North Africa until 1832.

But when Winslow Homer arrived on assignment from Harper's Weekly in 1868, the region was dominated by tourists, grand hotels, railroads, and well-groomed trails for walking and riding. Homer took a new approach in his depiction of the landscape, showing it instead as a stage for human activity, rather than as a sublime paradise.

shortDescription: Along with Impressionist painters Claude Monet and Alfred Sisley, Pissarro pursued the theme of snow throughout his career, producing nearly 100 “snow” paintings. In 1879 France experienced an extraordinarily severe winter, which Pissarro explored in this and other works painted at his home in Pontoise, 30 miles west of Paris. Here snow covers the ground, houses, and vegetation in a frothy coat that resulted from the artist’s vigorous brushwork.

title: The Grand Canal, Venice
shortDescription: Although he did not begin to paint views, or vedute , until he was in his mid-40s, Francesco Guardi became an accomplished practitioner in the genre. In this work, one of his most important early cityscapes, he depicted the mouth of the Grand Canal bustling with late-afternoon activity. The emotional tenor of Guardi’s vedute—seen here in the brooding, melancholy aura of the sky—distinguishes them from the works of his predecessors.

title: Himself
shortDescription: Robert Henri painted Himself and Herself (Irish terms of endearment for a husband and wife) during a summer trip to Ireland; the canvases depict the fisherman Johnnie Cummings and his wife, Biddy. The rich hues and thick, lush paint add depth to the works, while the figures’ elusive expressions and informal poses give them a brusque, forthright quality.

title: Saint James's Vision of the Virgin of the Pillar

shortDescription: In addition to large-scale portraits, James McNeill Whistler created small-scale likenesses, often on wood panel, as in this painting of a young sitter. A well-known beauty, Olga Caracciolo lived in Dieppe, France, likely where this work was executed, and later married the photographer Adolf de Meyer. Rather than a swift, abbreviated study for a larger composition, Whistler considered a work such as this to be a satisfying aesthetic whole.

title: Saint Romanus of Antioch and Saint Barulas
shortDescription: Francisco de Zurbarán created this painting for a church in Seville, Spain, dedicated to Saint Romanus of Antioch. Here, Romanus holds up his own tongue, torn out by his tormentors, and grasps a massive book inscribed with a prayer for the faithful. Painted to support the Counter-Reformation, the Catholic Church’s response to the Protestant movement, Zurbarán aimed to make the saints accessible to everyday people.

title: Bordighera
shortDescription: Monet created this painting in 1884 when he traveled to Bordighera, a town on the Italian Riviera. In a letter to sculptor Auguste Rodin, he described his efforts to capture the brilliant Mediterranean light, declaring that he was “fencing, wrestling, with the sun.” In this light-drenched composition painted from a hilltop vantage point, the sea is barely visible through the interlaced trunks of pine trees.

title: Virgil Reading the "Aeneid" to Augustus, Octavia, and Livia
shortDescription: In the late 18th centurly, the French Academy and artist Jacques-Louis David promoted Classical subjects in history paintings as moral exemplars for contemporary audiences. Here, Wicar, one of David's students, depicted the Roman emperor Augustus and his family listening to Virgil’s reading of his epic poem The Aeneid . The emotionally charged gestures of the family suggest that they identify with the heroic events of the poem.

title: Yellow Dancers (In the Wings)
shortDescription: Edgar Degas first painted dancers as an independent subject in 1871. He would go on to devote almost half his output as an artist to this subject, observing countless performances and rehearsals at the Paris Opéra. Here, he placed the viewer in the wings, as if among the elite opera subscribers who paid for the privilege to roam and socialize backstage.

title: The Last of New England—The Beginning of New Mexico
shortDescription: In this painting, Marsden Hartley depicted an imagined scene in which the fallen trees of a New England forest in the foreground transition to the golden hills of New Mexico beyond. Weary of the East Coast, Hartley spent 18 months in the Southwest in 1918–19, believing that he could find rejuvenation in nature. Here, thick black lines define the Southwestern landscape, which he saw as alive with expressive potential.

title: Madame François Buron
shortDescription: After his father’s death, the young David was raised by his uncle, architect François Buron, and his wife, Marie-Josèphe Fromont. Madame Buron was supportive of David’s desire to become a painter, in opposition to her husband’s wish that he study architecture. In this intimate early portrait, David presented his aunt looking up momentarily from her reading. Her glance suggests an affectionate bond between the painter and sitter.
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Albert J. Beveridge in memory of her mother, Abby Louise Spencer (Mrs. Augustus Eddy).

title: Fishing in Spring, the Pont de Clichy (Asnières)
shortDescription: This painting is set on the river Seine at the Clichy Bridge near Asnières, a suburb north of Paris where Van Gogh painted on several occasions with his friend and fellow artist Paul Signac. Van Gogh was inspired by a technique Signac innovated called divisionism, in which, using science-based color theory, he painted distinct strokes of different colors of paint next to each other to make each color more luminous.

title: Head of a Guillotined Man
shortDescription: This painting is one of several that Géricault produced of decapitated heads and severed limbs, and he likely painted it directly from life. The artist is known to have acquired corpses from his local morgue to study anatomy and the effects of decomposition. The head probably belonged to a convicted criminal. At that time in France, executions were carried out by the guillotine, a bladed device that sliced through the necks of its victims.

title: Peach Blossoms
shortDescription: Early in his career, Homer often depicted scenes of leisure, such as this young woman looking at peach blossoms. The setting itself reflects nostalgia for a fading rural past. Homer's use of a lighter palette was inspired by Impressionism, and the linearity of the tree is reminiscent of Japanese calligraphy. While critics often noted the innate American quality of Homer's work, this painting indicates the global artistic exchange of the time.

shortDescription: In 1891, as a result of his rheumatoid arthritis, Cross moved to the Côte d’Azur in southeastern France. The move deeply affected his art: after settling on the Mediterranean coast, he embraced the divided brushwork (small dashes and dots of color) and tonal gradations of “scientific Impressionism.” This methodical technique was a departure from the Impressionists’ more intuitive quick strokes of color to capture fleeting atmospheric conditions.

title: Watering Place at Marly
shortDescription: In 1875 Alfred Sisley moved to the French village of Marly-le-Roi. His home flanked the pool, or “watering place,” featured on the left of this canvas, which had once been the water gardens of King Louis XIV's country retreat. Sisley faithfully depicted landscapes throughout his career, spending most of his life painting in the villages along the Seine River, in the region referred to as the cradle of Impressionism.

title: Calf's Head and Ox Tongue
shortDescription: Caillebotte may have been inspired by the butcher’s shop below his family home in Paris when he painted this bloody scene of animal parts ready for human consumption. The painting confronts viewers with objects that are visually unpleasant and yet rendered with highly decorative pastel colors and soft brushstrokes.

title: The Prairie on Fire
shortDescription: Alvan Fisher was a pioneering American landscapist whose work offered a precedent for the Hudson River School. As a Romantic-era artist, Fisher preferred dramatic episodes, which involved striking contrasts between light and dark. In this version the prairie grasses are exquisitely rendered, and the figures are dwarfed by nature, underscoring both the landscape’s beauty as well as its dangers.

title: Major-General Henry Dearborn
shortDescription: Gilbert Stuart’s idealized portrayal of Major-General Henry Dearborn presents an aging, yet robust military leader. Dearborn was a Revolutionary War hero who was secretary of war during Thomas Jefferson’s two presidential terms (1801–09) and served as senior major-general in the War of 1812. This work is one of several portraits Stuart made of American military and political men, among them his well-known depictions of George Washington.

shortDescription: The subject of this painting, Marion Deering, was the wife of Charles Deering, a Chicago businessman, an important benefactor of the Art Institute, and Sargent's lifelong friend and patron. The broader handling of paint in her dress signals his facility with the tactile and expressive possibilities of paint.

title: Te raau rahi (The Big Tree)
shortDescription: “Everything in the landscape blinded and dazzled me,” wrote Paul Gauguin of his first months in Tahiti. Here, he showcased the island’s variety of bountiful fruit trees, including a thick-trunked, violet hotu at left; spindly mango and coconut trees; and three short banana plants with lush, splayed leaves. In the foreground, a man uses a stick to crack a coconut, and a family rests in the grass with a sleeping dog beside them.
